*The Complete Field Guide*

# **How To Read This Guide**

This guide uses generic placeholder names throughout so every example is easy to adapt to any character or system: {TrackerName} for a generic tracker, {MeterName} for a shared numeric meter, and NPCA / NPCB / NPCC when an example needs more than one character. Replace these with your own tracker names and character names when you copy an example into your own sheet.

**Confidence labels:** Every claim in this guide is marked one of three ways — CONFIRMED (tested directly, or confirmed by me asking the team), a design pattern (a recommended approach that has worked, but isn't the only valid one), or an open question (not yet tested — flagged so you know to verify it yourself before relying on it).

***![][image2]***

# **1\. What Is a Tracker?**

A Tracker is a small, independent state object built into the character sheet card, a native alternative to the old hidden-text tricks (writing state inside HTML comments or custom XML tags and hoping the model keeps it consistent). A Tracker remembers one specific piece of information about your story and updates it automatically as the chat progresses: a mood, a location, a relationship meter, a clock, a quest name, anything you define.

## **1.1 Anatomy of a Tracker**

| Field | What it does |
| :---- | :---- |
| Type | Text, Options, Meter, Number, Yes/No, or Time |
| Start | The seed/default value before anything happens |
| Update rules | Your instructions for how the value should change. 4000 character max. Read by a separate “state model,” not the main chat model directly. |
| Reads From | Toggle: Both (default) / User message / Character reply. Restricts which side of the exchange this tracker’s Update rules are evaluated against that turn. |
| Reference in text as | The {TrackerName} syntax used to pull this tracker's value into ED / APD / Personality |
| Reader sees value | Toggle: show this tracker's value in the user-facing chat HUD, or keep it hidden |
| User can edit state | Toggle: lets the user directly edit the visible HUD values |

✅ CONFIRMED: “Reads from” (per-tracker read scope) — every tracker has a toggle: Both (default), User message, or Character reply. It restricts which side of the exchange counts as a valid trigger for that tracker’s Update rules that turn; the other side’s content is not evaluated at all. In the Import/Export JSON this is the "evidence" field: "user" for User message only, "character" for Character reply only, and the key is omitted entirely for Both — real exports never write an explicit "both" string.

Design tip: use it to remove a category of ambiguity at the source. A tracker that should only ever move on something the user did (a consent flag, a user-initiated action counter) set to User message can no longer be nudged by the character’s own narration echoing that content back — and the same in reverse for character-only backstage state (an NPC’s private mood meter that shouldn’t react to the user’s meta-commentary).

✅ CONFIRMED: Sheet-level cap: maximum 24 trackers per character.

## **![][image3]**

## **1.2 HUD Display Formatting**

Some trackers show their value next to the label; others show it on the line below. This is intentional platform behavior, not a mistake in your setup:

* Text, Meters and Options trackers → value renders on a NEW line below the label (keeps the value from visually colliding with the label text).

* Number, Time, Yes/No→ value renders INLINE, next to the label, same line.

Design implication: don't try to shorten a Text/Options tracker's value to force it onto one line — it's structural, not about length. Plan your HUD layout expecting two lines per Text/Options/Meter tracker versus one line for the other types.

✅ CONFIRMED: Roughly 9-10 trackers are visible before the HUD panel needs scrolling. Combined with the 24-tracker cap, most of a fully-built sheet sits below the fold — order your trackers with the most important ones first.

## **1.3 Visibility & Authority — Which Fields Can See What**

The tracker system runs on **TWO separate models** operating in parallel. They do NOT share context — each sees a different slice of your sheet. Understanding this split is the single most important thing to know about building reliable trackers.:

#### **What the Tracker AI (state model) sees:**

* **Name, Description, Personality, APD, and ED.** — first \~4000 characters of each field only, as background context. Even within that window, the tracker AI is told NOT to treat these as binding update logic. They are passive reference, not authoritative instructions.  
* **Global "Tracking instructions" box** — read IN FULL, up to **4,000 characters**. This is the authoritative instruction space for the tracker AI.  
* **Each tracker's own Update rules / guidance field** — read IN FULL, up to **4,000 characters** per field.  
* **Scenario is NOT included.** (Squirtle confirmed: only a chat-scenario's premise is seen, and only when running a group chat/scenario.)

✅ CONFIRMED: Update logic belongs in the tracker system (Tracking instructions box \+ per-field guidance), NOT in APD/ED. References in Name, Description, Personality, APD, and ED fieldes beyond \~4000 chars per field are invisible to the tracker AI. Even within that window, they are treated as passive background — not binding instructions.

⚠️ ROOT CAUSE of "runaway meter" reports: Modifier definitions placed in Extra Details were \~97% invisible to the tracker AI, which improvised category meanings with no definitions to constrain it. Moving definitions to the global Tracking instructions box (4,000 chars, read in full) fixed drift entirely in squirtle's own replay tests — "Sure / ok / go on" messages stayed flat; legitimate actions still advanced the meter.

#### **What the Chat Model sees:**

* **APD / ED / Scenario / Personality / Greeting, etc.** — in full, as normal.  
* **Tracker guidance / update rules / Tracking instructions** — **NONE.** The chat model never sees any tracker logic, modifier definitions, or update rules.  
* **Current tracker values** — a synthesized block like `"Anchor: 12/100, Mood: tense"` covering every field, **including fields with "Reader sees value" turned OFF.** Turning off visibility hides the HUD display from users — NOT the value from the chat model.

**Critical implication:** the chat model has no idea WHY a tracker has a certain value — only what it is. If you want the chat model to understand the meaning of a value (e.g. "Depth Level 3 \= guarded flirtation"), that explanation must live in APD/ED. The tracker guidance explaining it never reaches the chat model.

#### 

#### 

#### 

#### **The two supported integration patterns:**

**Pattern 1 — Reference tracker values from APD/ED:** Use `{Field Label}` tokens in your character fields. The chat model resolves them to the current value silently. This is the designed integration point.

**⚠️**  Exception confirmed 2026-08-03: this resolves against the label text VERBATIM (case-insensitive, spaces/punctuation preserved) — UNLESS the label carries an emoji, in which case the platform silently sanitizes it to a snake\_case key instead, and THAT sanitized form is what actually resolves, not the visible label. Example: a tracker labeled "Affection Harper" resolves as {Affection Harper}; a tracker labeled "💛 Affection Harper" resolves only as {affection\_harper}. Simplest safe practice: If you put an emoji on any tracker’s label, double check that you are referencing it by {field\_label} and not {Field Label} in the sheet.

**Pattern 2 — Descriptive enum option names:** Name your Options tracker values descriptively (e.g. "Guarded Flirtation" instead of "Level 3") so the value itself carries meaning to the chat model — since it sees the value but not the definition behind it.

⚠️ Anti-pattern to avoid: Writing modifier definitions or update logic in APD/ED and expecting the tracker AI to respect them as binding rules. Within the first 4000 chars they're visible as passive background; beyond that they're invisible entirely.

🔧 Debug exception: The character's author can type /analyze in their own chat to get a debug view where the chat model IS shown the full tracker definitions — useful for diagnosing "why did the tracker do X?" This is author-only, not visible to regular users.

⚠️ Native Trackers vs Manual STATE Blocks: Running native trackers simultaneously with an old ED-based STATE block architecture (e.g. \<S\> blocks, `<!-- –->` syntax, any instruction requiring the character to print a state block in every reply) causes the two systems to conflict. The native tracker replaces the manual STATE block function entirely — remove old manual state-block instructions from ED when migrating to native trackers.

## **1.4 Builder Toolbar**

The tracker builder's overflow menu (•••) provides:

* Import — opens a paste box for raw JSON. You'll be asked to choose “Replace current tracker” or “Add to existing fields” before committing.

* Export — copies the full tracker set's JSON straight to your clipboard.

* Save all as preset — names and saves every current field on the sheet as one reusable bundle.

* Library — lists your saved presets by name and field count, with a “+” to add a preset into the current character and a trash icon to delete it.

* Show all in chat — see warning below.

⚠️  “Show all in chat” is a bulk override, not a preview. It force-sets EVERY tracker to visible and relabels itself “Hide all.” There is no automatic revert — if triggered by accident, you'll need to manually re-hide each tracker back to your intended layout.

✅ CONFIRMED: Import/Export preserves the FULL content of every field, including your complete Update rules text — not just the tracker's basic shell (type/name/min-max). A validated multi-tracker system is genuinely portable: build it once, export it, and reuse it on future characters.

## ***![][image6]***

## **1.5 Preview Panels**

The builder provides two live preview panes, useful for debugging without any extra setup:

* “What the user sees” — mirrors the real in-chat HUD. Only shows trackers whose “Reader sees value” toggle is ON.

* “Internal state (sent to the chat model)” — shows the raw payload actually delivered to the chat model every message, regardless of each tracker's visibility toggle. This includes trackers hidden from the user entirely.

✅ CONFIRMED: Long Text-type values are visually truncated with “…” in the Internal State panel — this is a UI display limit only. The full, untruncated value is what the chat model actually receives.

# **2\. The \#1 Failure Mode: Ambiguity Kills Updates**

This is the single most important debugging lesson in this guide.

**The symptom:** an Options tracker meant to track who's currently speaking — call it {ActiveSpeaker}, with possible values NPCA / NPCB / NPCC — can simply stop updating the moment more than one character can speak within the same response. A rule like this looks reasonable at first:

Change {ActiveSpeaker} to whoever spoke last.

This works fine when only one character responds per message. The moment your scene design allows two or three characters to speak in the same message, the tracker has no reliable way to determine “who spoke last” — and when the model is unsure, it appears to fail CLOSED: it holds the previous value instead of guessing. It just quietly stops updating.

**The fix: replace interpretation with mechanical parsing.**

Identify the party member with the LAST dialogue line in the most recently completed response. A dialogue line \= plain text preceded by "Name:" per the sheet's format. Narration/actions in \*asterisks\* do NOT count as speaking.  
   
Scan the response from END backward to START. Set {ActiveSpeaker} to the first character name found attached to a dialogue line in that backward scan — i.e. whoever's spoken line is closest to the end of the response.  
   
IF no character has a dialogue line this response (pure narration, nobody spoke): do not change {ActiveSpeaker} — hold the previous value.  
IF multiple characters have dialogue: set to whichever line is LAST in reading order — not whoever speaks most, not whoever speaks first.

**The general principle:** any time your instruction uses a fuzzy word like “recent,” “whoever,” or “the last one,” define it with a literal, format-based rule (a text prefix, a keyword, a structural marker) instead of trusting the model to infer it. This gets MORE important as your scene complexity grows — a rule that works fine on day one can quietly stop working later once scenes get busier, with no error to warn you.

***![][image8]***

# **3\. How Trackers Update — By Design, Not a Bug**

This is confirmed platform behavior (via the Tracker feedback channel during beta tests), and it explains a lot of otherwise-confusing tracker behavior once it clicks.

**The actual per-message flow:**

* 1\. Evaluate current tracker values (as they stood at the end of the PREVIOUS message)

* 2\. The Chat model generates this response using those values

* 3\. The response is printed

* 4\. THEN Tracker Model values update, based on what just happened in the response that was printed

✅ CONFIRMED: The model writing message N is always reading tracker state as of the end of message N-1 (minus one). This is a deliberate, current design of the platform, not a bug to report, and not something ED/tracker logic can override. Plan around it rather than trying to “fix” it.

## **3.1 The “-1 Offset” Rule**

Any threshold condition that used to fire “when the counter reaches X” needs to fire at X-1 (minus one) instead. Reasoning: at the moment the model reads a value of 99 and writes its response, the tracker is about to become 100 right after — which is exactly the message where you want the “counter hit 100” payoff to appear. Wait for the tracker to literally show 100 first, and the payoff shows up one full message late.

**Rule of thumb when designing any threshold-based tracker: subtract 1 from every trigger threshold.**

## **3.2 This Applies To Every Field, Not Just Tracker-to-Tracker**

The chat model itself, reading a {TrackerName} substitution inside ED / APD / Scenario while writing the current response, is also always seeing the PREVIOUS message's resolved value. This is not a special case limited to one tracker depending on another — any field on the sheet that references a tracker is subject to the same one-message lag.

## **3.3 A Concrete Consequence: Derived Trackers Can Lag Visually**

Say {ActiveSpeaker} (Section 2\) drives a second tracker, {OutfitTracker}, that resolves the currently-speaking character's visual description — injected into an image-generation tag at the top of every response. Directly tested consequence:

✅ CONFIRMED: If {ActiveSpeaker} was NPCA going into a response, and that response's dialogue ends with NPCB speaking (so {ActiveSpeaker} becomes NPCB AFTER the response prints), {OutfitTracker} in that SAME response still resolved to NPCA's description — because it read {ActiveSpeaker} as it stood BEFORE the response, not after. An image generated off that response's tag will show the wrong character for that one beat. The correct values only appear starting the NEXT response.

**Mitigation options (pick based on your use case — none is universally “the” fix):**

* Option A — Accept the lag, generate one message later. Don't generate on the message where the speaker changes; generate on the following message once the dependent tracker has caught up. Zero new logic, costs a one-message delay.

* Option B — Predict instead of read. Rewrite the dependent tracker to independently re-derive “who's closing THIS response” using the same backward-scan logic as Section 2, instead of depending on the other tracker's stale value. Risk: duplicates the parsing logic across two trackers, doubling the surface area for Section 2's ambiguity failure.

None of these options eliminate the core lag from Section 3 — they only change how gracefully a dependent system degrades around it.

In the capture below, the last Active Character was Kaelith (the red haired warrior) but in this response the last to speak was Elandra (the blonde elf mage) as you can see by the end of the response the tracker updated “Active member” but since the last was Kaelith that value still holds in the response and when I clicked Generate I got an image of Kaelith.

## **3.4 Tracker Position Also Affects Update Reliability In Large Sets**

The order in which trackers are positioned in the UI matters, trackers whose values are important for others to update should be positioned first (top) of the ones that depend on its value, for example if you have an outfit tracker that is location dependent, the location tracker must be above the outfit tracker.

## **✅ CONFIRMED:** This comes from a production incident (a 21-tracker character): trackers positioned late in a large \`fields\` array can silently stop updating even while everything earlier in the array works fine — not the N−1 lag from Section 3 (which is position-independent; every tracker already reads last turn’s state regardless of array order), a distinct effect. In the incident, two foundational "lock" trackers sitting 2nd-to-last and last in a 21-field array never fired — along with everything gated behind them — until moved to the very front of the array. Small sets seem unaffected: House\_Base-style 8-tracker sets with a display tracker reading four OTHER trackers defined after it in the array have worked reliably since first tested. Practical rule: in any set pushing toward the 24-tracker cap, place one-time locks, arrival/unlock gates, and anything a lot of other logic depends on toward the FRONT of the array — don’t just append new trackers to the end as a set grows. This can cost a little HUD-cosmetic ordering; that tradeoff is worth it.

# **4\. Numeric Meters: Two Valid Design Patterns**

For Meter and Number trackers, don't let the value increment by default every turn — force a classification step first, or the number stops meaning anything.

## **4.1 Pattern A — Classification-Before-Range**

Best for narrative/qualitative progress (a quest, an objective, anything that should feel earned rather than mechanically farmed):

Classify the latest action against the current objective:  
IF unrelated (banter, downtime, unrelated exploration): no change.  
ELIF PREPARATORY (scouting, gathering intel/tools, planning with the  
     objective explicitly in mind): \+5 to \+10.  
ELIF DIRECT (actively executes toward the objective, confronts the  
     obstacle/target): \+15 to \+30, scaled to impact.  
ELIF the narrative EXPLICITLY resolves the objective this turn (a  
     clear stated outcome, not implied): SET \= 100\.  
   
CAP: Talk/planning ABOUT the objective without a real action taken  
is PREPARATORY at most, never DIRECT. Cap cumulative discussion-only  
gains at \+10 total until a real action occurs.  
   
COMPLETION: Never infer from tone, confidence, or stated intent.  
"We're ready to attack" is NOT complete. "The camp burns, the enemy  
falls" IS complete.

✅ CONFIRMED: The completion standard above is the single highest-leverage rule in a progress-type tracker — it's the difference between a meter that tracks real narrative progress and one that fills up the first time anyone sounds confident.

Because of Section 3's lag, a natural companion rule is to hold a resolved value (like 100\) for one extra message before resetting, rather than assuming the next tracker in the chain will see the new value immediately:

RESET: Hold the meter at 100 the turn it's reached. On the NEXT  
turn, once the dependent objective-name tracker has rotated to the  
new objective, reset to 0\.

## **4.2 Pattern B — Explicit Gain/Loss Table**

Best when you need precise, reproducible point values tied to specific named triggers — the same style long used in ED-only Trust/Love meters before native trackers existed:

\+5 if \[specific trigger A\]  
\+10 if \[specific trigger B\]  
\-5 if \[specific trigger C\]

✅ CONFIRMED: Both patterns are valid inputs to the same 4000-character Update rules field. Which to use is a granularity choice, not a platform constraint.

## 

## 

## **4.3 Multi-State Selection (Driven By Another Tracker \+ Context)**

A common pattern for something like an outfit/appearance state that should shift with scene context:

Read {ActiveSpeaker} to select the base character.  
IF combat active/imminent, or executing the mission objective: use  
     her "Field" set.  
ELIF an explicit sexual act is ACTIVELY occurring this turn (not  
     implied, not foreplay-only): use her "Nude" set.  
ELIF relaxed downtime, no threat present: use her "Casual" set.  
ELSE: hold the previous value — do not guess when context is  
     ambiguous.

“Hold on ambiguity” is a deliberate, recurring safety pattern — it shows up across every reliable tracker built this way.

![][image10]

# **5\. Multi-Value (Options) Trackers**

Options trackers support multiple simultaneously-active values, several chips lit up at once in the HUD (e.g. a tracker holding several active story flags at the same time).

Note: This Section covers the multi-value Options tracker only (JSON type: multi\_enum) — the kind where several items can be active simultaneously, using ADD/REMOVE/CONTAINS syntax. The single-choice Options tracker (JSON type: enum, where only one value is active at a time) works like any other Options field: just set the value directly in your Update rules. No ADD/REMOVE needed. The two types look similar in the UI but are distinct in the schema — if you only need one active value at a time, use the single-choice version and keep the rules simple.

![][image11]

**The set-operation convention (no confirmed native syntax exists, so this is an adopted, tested convention):**

IF {TrackerName} CONTAINS "ItemName": \[condition\]  
IF {TrackerName} NOT CONTAINS "ItemName": \[condition\]  
ADD "ItemName" TO {TrackerName}  
REMOVE "ItemName" FROM {TrackerName}

⚠️  Never instruct a full “SET {TrackerName} \= …” overwrite of a multi-value tracker — this forces the model to re-list every currently-active item from memory each turn, a strong candidate for silently dropping items. Always ADD/REMOVE individual elements.

## **⚠️**  Confirmed 2026-08-02 from a production incident: the \`initial\` value for a multi\_enum field must be a JSON array — \`\[\]\` or \`\["ItemName"\]\` — never a bare string. A bare-string initial doesn’t just fail for that one field: it silently froze the ENTIRE tracker set (21 fields, none updating) for the affected character, with no error shown anywhere in the builder UI. This is one of the highest-severity JSON mistakes to check for before importing any set that includes a multi\_enum field.

## 

## **5.1 Confirmed Via Isolated Mechanism Testing**

To separate “does the set mechanism work” from “can the model correctly decide WHEN to fire it,” the convention above was tested using literal test commands instead of narrative triggers:

| \# | Action | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | ADD ItemA | ✅ ItemA active |
| 2 | ADD ItemA again | ✅ ItemA active, no duplicate |
| 3 | ADD ItemB | ✅ ItemA, ItemB both active |
| 4 | REMOVE ItemA | ✅ ItemB only, ItemA cleanly removed |
| 5 | REMOVE ItemC (not active) | ✅ no change, no corruption |
| 6 | ADD ItemD \+ ADD ItemE, same message | ✅ both added in one turn |
| 7 | Ambient turn, no command | ✅ unchanged, persists |
| 8 | CLEAR | ✅ empty |

✅ CONFIRMED: 8/8 mechanism tests passed. The ADD/REMOVE/CONTAINS convention is reliable for the mechanics themselves. This does NOT validate narrative classification accuracy — deciding WHEN to fire ADD/REMOVE from an inferred scene event is the same class of problem as Section 2's ambiguity failure, and remains a separate, case-by-case concern to test.

📌 Mechanical nuance (confirmed by squirtle): The ADD/REMOVE/CONTAINS convention works, but under the hood the tracker AI is asked to emit the full updated list each time — ADD/REMOVE phrasing in your rules is translated by the model into list operations, not executed as atomic commands. The convention remains valid and tested, but this is useful to know when debugging unexpected item drops: if items are disappearing, the failure point is the model not reconstructing the full list correctly, not a broken ADD/REMOVE operation.

# **6\. Yes/No Trackers**

Renders as a checkbox in the HUD (checked \= Yes, unchecked \= No) rather than as text — consistent with Section 1.2's rule that Number/Time/Yes-No types render inline/compact.

Tested with the same isolated-mechanism approach as Section 5:

| \# | Action | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | No command | ✅ holds default |
| 2 | SET YES | ✅ Yes |
| 3 | Ambient turn | ✅ Yes, unchanged |
| 4 | SET YES again | ✅ Yes, idempotent |
| 5 | TOGGLE | ✅ No |
| 6 | TOGGLE | ✅ Yes, symmetric |
| 7 | SET NO | ✅ No |
| 8 | Both SET YES and SET NO in same message | ✅ LAST instruction wins |

✅ CONFIRMED: 8/8 passed. Reliable for basic set/toggle/persist mechanics.

**Notable finding from \#8:** conflict resolution here differs from Section 2's failure mode. Genuine ambiguity (multiple valid candidates, no clear signal) appears to fail closed — holding the previous value. Two directly conflicting EXPLICIT instructions in the same message did NOT hold the previous value — the tracker took the LAST instruction as authoritative. If you need a specific instruction to win regardless of message order, don't rely on placement — write an explicit precedence rule (e.g. “if both conditions are present, X always overrides Y”).

# **7\. Time Trackers**

A fixed 24-hour clock (HH:MM). Confirmed working with a scene-weight classification pattern:

Classify the response:  
IF OOC/meta only: no change.  
ELIF a quick exchange/short beat: \+2 to \+10 min.  
ELIF a normal scene (conversation, nearby movement, a shared task):  
     \+15 to \+40 min.  
ELIF an extended scene (full conversation, travel, a meal, an  
     intimate scene, combat): \+40 to \+90 min.  
ELIF the narrative explicitly states a skip ("next morning", "X  
     hours later"): set directly, overriding the ranges above.  
   
WRAP RULE: crossing 24:00 wraps to 00:00. This tracker holds  
time-of-day only — it has no memory of which day it is.  
   
AGENCY GUARD: never use time advancement to auto-skip a scene,  
auto-separate characters, or force an ending. An explicit user  
skip request always overrides the default ranges.

✅ CONFIRMED: Pairing a Time tracker with a separate tracker for date memory (a Number tracker for a numeric day/month/year, or an Options/Text tracker for a named day-of-week/month) is a confirmed, valid approach for full date+time tracking — not a workaround. The date tracker's Update rules would increment when the Time tracker wraps past 24:00, cross-referenced the same way any dependent tracker reads another (Section 3).

# **8\. Shared Meter Driving Multiple Derived Trackers**

**The correct mental model for this pattern:** APD/ED and the tracker system serve two different audiences with two different jobs — neither can do the other's work, but they communicate through {tracker} value tokens.

**Tracker Update rules / Tracking instructions** → define **when and how the value changes**. Read by the tracker AI. This is where update logic lives.

**APD/ED** → define **what a value means for the character's behavior**. Read by the chat model. This is where behavioral instructions live.

{TrackerName} **token in APD/ED** → the bridge. The chat model resolves it to the current value and uses whatever APD says that value means.

This is not a budget workaround — it is the correct architecture for behavioral state. Putting behavioral prose in a tracker field wastes space on the wrong audience. Putting update logic in APD risks it being treated as passive background by the tracker AI (which only sees \~4000 chars of each field, as background, not as instructions — Section 1.3).

## **8.1 The Pattern**

* One shared Meter tracker, `{SynergyMeter}` (0-100), tracks a single group-wide value. Its own Update rules stay minimal — a sentence or two about what raises or lowers it.

* Several short Text trackers (`{NPCA_Status}`, `{NPCB_Status}`...) each hold a brief derived label (e.g. 2 words / 30 chars max). Their Update rules say "derive this label from the current phase based on `{SynergyMeter}`."

* APD holds the full behavioral document per character, using the `{SynergyMeter}` token directly:


PHASE 1 — (0–30)  
Behavior: \[how the character acts at this phase\]  
Key tells: \[physical/dialogue tells\]  
Forbidden Action: \[what she will NOT do — keeps transitions subtle\]  
   
PHASE 2 — (31–60)  
Trigger event: \[narrative trigger\]  
Behavior: \[...\]  
Forbidden action: \[explicit negative constraint to keep the  
     transition subtle rather than an obvious mood-swing\]  
   
PHASE 3 — (61–89)  
...  
   
PHASE 4 — (90+)  
...

✅ CONFIRMED: A single tracker can be referenced from more than one field simultaneously (e.g. both APD and ED) — multi-field cross-referencing is supported. `{Field Label}` token references are **case-insensitive** in the code (exact match is still good practice, but a mismatch won't break it).

## **8.2 Why This Works Better For Narrative State**

The phase-band logic is inherently something the chat model also needs to know — it's driving actual roleplay behavior and tone, not just something the tracker model needs to compute a label from. Writing it once in APD serves double duty: it shapes the narrative AND gives the tracker model enough surrounding context to derive the short label correctly, without duplicating the full spec inside several separate 4000-character tracker fields.

**When to use this pattern versus Section 4's classification-in-tracker approach:**

* Purely mechanical/backstage state (nobody needs the chat model to reason about it directly) → keep the logic in the tracker's own field.

* Narrative/behavioral state that should visibly shape how a character acts → put the substance in APD/ED where the chat model reads it anyway, and let the tracker's own field be a thin pointer.  
  The tracker holds the number. The APD holds what that number means narratively.

⚠️ Important constraint (confirmed): The phase definitions in APD shape what the CHAT MODEL does — but the TRACKER AI cannot reliably use them as binding update logic. APD content beyond \~1,500 chars is invisible to the tracker AI, and even within that window it's treated as background, not instructions. If a derived label tracker (e.g. {NPCA\_Status}) needs to know what Phase 2 means to compute its label correctly, those definitions must ALSO live in the global Tracking instructions box (4,000 chars) — not only in APD.

The tracker holds the number. APD tells the chat model what that number means. The Tracking instructions box tells the tracker AI what that number means. These are three different jobs.

## **8.3 Watch Out For Drift**

⚠️  Real inconsistency caught during testing: an ED independently redefined the SAME mechanic's threshold that was already defined in APD — different phase number, different percentage, same event, two fields. When a mechanic's thresholds are defined in one field, do NOT redefine those same specific numbers independently in another field — reference the already-defined system by name/trigger only, or keep a single field as the sole source of truth for the actual values. Reinforcing a rule's EXISTENCE across multiple fields is good practice; redefining its SPECIFIC VALUES independently in each field is not — that's duplication, not reinforcement, and it's exactly what drifts.

Because of Section 3's lag, a phase transition may narrate the OLD phase for one extra message after the meter numerically crosses a boundary — the same “-1 offset” logic likely applies to phase-band boundaries too if landing the transition exactly on the threshold-crossing message matters. Not yet confirmed for this specific case — flagged as an open question.

## **8.4 Meter Colors**

✅ CONFIRMED: Fixed palette: Pink, Red, Green, or a fixed Pink-to-Green Gradient. No custom color picker exists yet.

# **![][image13]**

# **9\. Common Bug: Trackers Leaking Into Narrative Text**

With native trackers rendering their own HUD automatically, the chat model sometimes ALSO prints the same state as narrative prose inside the actual response — duplicating the HUD display. Example of what this looks like when it goes wrong:

Synergy: 100/100  
Party Connection: High  
NPCA Respect: Vulnerable and Hopeful

...appearing as visible text inside the character's actual dialogue/narration, not just in the HUD where it belongs.

**Fix — add this near the top of your ED, at your highest enforcement priority:**  
**(if you want to fix it)**

TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK  
Tracker values are rendered automatically by the platform HUD — NEVER by narrative text.  
   
NEVER write tracker names/values/labels as visible prose or bullet lists in the response body. This includes:  
\- Bullet-point or list-style summaries of state  
\- Restating a stat's current label or number inline in narration or dialogue  
\- Any HUD-style readout duplicated inside the narrative, in any format  
   
Narrative may REFLECT underlying state through prose, tone, and character behavior — but must NEVER cite the tracker's label or value directly, anywhere in the response.  
   
SELF-CHECK before sending: scan the response for any line matching a "Label: Value" or "Label: Number/Number" pattern, or any bullet list summarizing state. IF found: delete it.

✅ CONFIRMED: The literal pattern-match self-check is the load-bearing part of this rule — it gives the model something concrete to search for before sending, not just a vague “don't show the HUD.”

![][image14]

# **10\. Debugging: How To See What Your Trackers Are Actually Doing**

Both preview panels in the builder (Section 1.5) are the first place to check — they let you see resolved tracker values without touching the live chat at all. For checking values in the middle of an actual conversation, a temporary debug line is the most reliable approach.

**Temporary debug pattern — add to ED, remove once you're done testing:**

DEBUG\_TRACKER\_PROBE — TEMPORARY, SUPERSEDES TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK  
This is an authorized diagnostic exception to TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK,  
active only while this block is present in ED. Remove entirely once  
testing is complete.  
   
At the absolute end of every response, output as the final VISIBLE  
line of plain text (NOT wrapped in XML/hidden-state tags, NOT an  
HTML comment):  
   
DEBUG PROBE — TrackerA=\[value\] | TrackerB=\[value\]  
   
Recognize this line specifically by the literal prefix "DEBUG  
PROBE —" and never delete/hide/move a line starting with that  
exact prefix, regardless of what TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK otherwise  
instructs.  
   
IF a value resolves to empty/unset: write "UNRESOLVED" instead of  
omitting the line.

**Three lessons baked into this pattern:**

* Never use ALL-CAPS XML-style tags for anything meant to be VISIBLE. That formatting is the established convention for HIDDEN state on this kind of sheet and tends to get treated accordingly — wrapping visible debug output in tags like that can cause it to simply not render.

* Use a distinct literal text prefix (not colon-based “Label: Value”) so the debug line doesn't collide with your own TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK self-check from Section 9 and get deleted.

* Always report UNRESOLVED explicitly rather than omitting the line — silence during debugging is indistinguishable from “this rule didn't run at all.”

⚠️  Treat this pattern as strictly temporary. Leaving it active in production reintroduces the exact leak that TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK exists to prevent.

# **11\. A Note On Reliability: Escape Hatches Get Over-Used**

This lesson came from a mandatory image-tag injection rule, but it applies to any strict, always-required instruction tied to tracker output.

An early version of a mandatory rule included a conditional skip path: “if the value is empty, skip this step.” In testing, the model over-used that escape hatch — the step was randomly skipped even when the tracker value WAS present, especially on low-signal/ambient turns where the model seemed to reach for the easiest exit.

**The fix: remove all conditional skip paths from a truly mandatory rule.**

* Always output SOMETHING — a defined fallback value beats an absent output entirely.

* Add an explicit self-check step (“is this literally the first/last thing in the response? If no, rewrite”) rather than trusting the instruction to be followed once, unreinforced.

⚠️  General principle: don't give the model permission to omit output on ambiguous/unresolved tracker state in a rule you consider non-negotiable. Always define a fallback instead — escape hatches get used more than intended, especially the further a conversation runs.

# **12\. JSON Export Schema**

Exporting a tracker set produces real JSON you can inspect, back up, or hand-edit. Here's a confirmed, generic-example structure:

{  
  "ourdreamTracker": 1,  
  "fields": \[  
    {  
      "key": "meter\_name",  
      "type": "meter",  
      "label": "MeterName",  
      "min": 0,  
      "max": 100,  
      "initial": 10,  
      "color": "purple",  
      "visible": true,  
      "guidance": "..."  
    },  
    {  
      "key": "active\_speaker",  
      "type": "enum",  
      "label": "Active Speaker",  
      "initial": "NPCA",  
      "options": \["NPCA", "NPCB", "NPCC"\],  
      "visible": true,  
      "guidance": "..."  
    },  
    {  
      "key": "test\_flag",  
      "type": "boolean",  
      "label": "TestFlag",  
      "initial": true,  
      "visible": true,  
      "guidance": "..."  
    }  
  \],  
  "userEditable": false  
}

**Confirmed internal type-name mapping — the JSON type value doesn't always match the UI button label:**

| UI label | JSON “type” value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Text | text |
| Options (single) | enum  |
| Options (multi) | multi\_enum |
| Meter | meter (adds min / max / color) |
| Number | counter — NOT “number” |
| Yes/No | boolean |
| Time | time |

* guidance \= your Update rules text (the full content, not a shell/reference).

* maxLength \= a SEPARATE cap on the tracker's own OUTPUT value length (e.g. 30 characters for a two-word label) — different from the 4000-character cap on the guidance field itself.

* visible maps to “Reader sees value.”

⚠️  \- The "color": "purple" in the JSON export \= Gradient. Same thing, different name.

**A useful technique found in a real export: embedding literal chat-command overrides directly inside a Number/counter tracker's own guidance, for quick production debugging without a separate debug tracker:**

if user types \#lower set {ProgressTracker} value:50  
if user types \#higher set {ProgressTracker} value:80

**✅ CONFIRMED:** Global Tracking Instructions can ship as a top-level \`"instructions"\` string key inside the SAME importable JSON — \`{"ourdreamTracker":1,"fields":\[...\],"instructions":"...","userEditable":false}\` — and it imports automatically along with the fields. Confirmed 2026-08-03 from a live export.

# **13\. Pre-Flight Checklist**

RRun through this before considering any tracker “done”:

●      Does the Update rules field define EXACTLY how to detect a change — no vague words like “recent” or “whoever” left unresolved? (Section 2\)

●      Is there an explicit “no relevant change → do nothing” branch, rather than incrementing/changing by default every message?

●      If this tracker depends on another tracker, have you accounted for the one-message lag (Section 3)? Have threshold conditions been offset by \-1 where needed?

●      If your tracker uses modifier definitions or gate rules that the tracker AI must treat as binding, have you placed them in the global Tracking instructions box — not just in ED/APD/Personality? *Rules in ED/APD beyond \~4000 chars per field are invisible to the tracker AI.* (Section 1.3)

●      If this is a progress/completion-style meter, is completion gated on an EXPLICIT, unambiguous outcome — never inferred from tone or stated intent? (Section 4\)

●      If a mechanic's exact thresholds are defined in one field (e.g. APD), have you avoided redefining those same specific numbers independently anywhere else? (Section 8.3)

●      Have you added a TRACKER\_OUTPUT\_LOCK-style rule if any of these trackers show up in the visible HUD, to prevent narrative leak? (Section 9\)

●      Have you actually tested this tracker a few times in a real chat — ideally with an isolated mechanism test (literal commands) BEFORE a narrative/ambiguity test, so you know which one broke if something fails? (Sections 5 & 6\)

If this tracker set is large (pushing toward the 24-tracker cap), are one-time locks, arrival/unlock gates, and anything else depends on placed toward the TOP of the list, not appended at the end? Tracker position affects update reliability separately from the N−1 lag. (Section 3.4)  
If this tracker set includes a multi\_enum field, is its \`initial\` a JSON array and never a bare string? A bare string can silently freeze the WHOLE set, not just this field. (Section 5\)

# **14\. Open Questions**

Not yet resolved — flagged here so nobody mistakes them for confirmed facts. If you test any of these, let me know so I can update.

* Does the phase-band transition lag (Section 8.3) actually show up in practice — does a shared-meter transition narrate the OLD phase for one extra message after crossing a threshold?

* Does a “STATE CHECK” style structured format (naming sub-signals with closed value sets, then a threshold rule) outperform plain IF/ELIF prose for reliability, or was an early example that seemed to work just a coincidence of being unusually well-specified?

* Does self-check compliance (Sections 9 & 11\) decay over very long chat sessions, the way other long-context instructions are known to?

* What explains the “color” field exporting as “purple” for a Meter tracker when the UI only shows four swatches? (Section 12\)

  * solved. The UI's "Gradient" color option is stored as purple in the schema. Same thing, two names.

* Does Import correctly preserve cross-tracker references (one tracker's guidance mentioning another tracker's {name}) when moved to a brand-new character, or only within the same sheet?

  * Mostly yes, one trap. References live as plain text in rules, so they survive. But import re-derives field keys from labels, so anything keyed off a stable internal key isn't stable across import — label-based references are the safe form (which the guide already recommends).

**Newly Confirmed Since First Publication:**

✅ CONFIRMED (squirtle): The tracker AI only sees the first 4000 chars of each character field (Name, Description, Personality, APD, and ED.) as background context only — not as binding update logic. The global Tracking instructions box (4,000 chars) and each tracker's own Update rules field (4,000 chars) are read in full as authoritative instructions. See updated Section 1.3.

✅ CONFIRMED: The chat model NEVER sees tracker update rules, modifier definitions, or Tracking instructions — only the current values. To help the chat model understand what a value means, put the explanation in APD/ED. See updated Section 1.3.

✅ CONFIRMED: Running native trackers simultaneously with old manual STATE block architecture in ED (e.g. \<S\> blocks, $$\[ syntax) causes the two systems to conflict. Remove old manual state-block instructions from ED when migrating to native trackers.

**✅ CONFIRMED (2026-08-02):** A \`multi\_enum\` field’s \`initial\` must be a JSON array, never a bare string — a bare string silently freezes the ENTIRE tracker set for that character, not just the one field. See updated Section 5 and Section 12\.  
   
**✅ CONFIRMED (2026-08-03):** \`{Field Label}\` token resolution matches the label text verbatim (case-insensitive) UNLESS the label carries an emoji, in which case it silently resolves against a sanitized snake\_case key instead. Never put an emoji on a label you plan to reference anywhere. See updated Section 1.3.  
   
**✅ CONFIRMED (2026-08-03):** A tracker’s position in the UI and  \`fields\` array affects how reliably it updates in LARGE sets (confirmed at 21 trackers; — a distinct effect from the N−1 lag. Place foundational/gating trackers near the front of the array. See new Section 3.4.  
   
**✅ CONFIRMED (2026-08-03):** A display/summary tracker that reconstructs its value every turn from several OTHER trackers (e.g. a one-line calendar header assembled from Day/Weekday/Date/Clock/Location) should recompute UNCONDITIONALLY, every turn — adding a "no-op if none of the source trackers changed" clause (which the general Section 2 no-op guidance would otherwise recommend) has been confirmed, live, to make this specific style of tracker stop updating. This is a deliberate exception to the general no-op rule, not an oversight.  
   
**✅ CONFIRMED (2026-08-03):** Global Tracking Instructions can ship as a top-level \`"instructions"\` key inside the same importable tracker JSON and import automatically — no manual paste into the separate builder field required. See updated Section 12\.
